sandhi.note: Final t before the palatal c becomes the palatal c: केचित् च → केचिच्च.
The t of केचित् stays unvoiced before p; final n before t becomes ṃs (पाशान् तथा → पाशांस्तथा); ā + a → ā (तथा अपरे → तथापरे).

sandhi.rule: visarga kept before s (the optional alternative to विसर्जनीयस्य सः, 8.3.34)
sandhi.note: Before an initial sibilant the visarga may stand or be assimilated (युयुधुस्संयुगे); the Gita Press keeps it.

samasa.sense: two kinds of edged weapon: the battle-axe and the paṭṭiśa, a spear or long blade with a sharp edge

morph.note: √युध् is ātmanepadin (युध्यते; perfect युयुधे, as in 2.41 and 2.43). The plural here takes the parasmaipada ending -उः instead of the classical युयुधिरे — the usual epic and Purāṇic form, used again in 2.53 and 2.63.
Perfect with reduplication: क्षि → चि (a guttural in the reduplicated syllable becomes the corresponding palatal), then the weak stem क्षिप् with -उः.

mantras.anvaya: (ते महासुराः तोमरैः भिन्दिपालैः च शक्तिभिः मुसलैः तथा) खड्गैः परशुपट्टिशैः (च) संयुगे देव्या (सह) युयुधुः। केचित् च शक्तीः चिक्षिपुः, केचित् पाशान् (चिक्षिपुः); तथा अपरे —
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line completes the sentence begun in 2.47b (तोमरैः … मुसलैः तथा): the list of instruments runs across the verse boundary. The second line distributes the action: ‘some … some … and others’; अपरे is taken as the subject of 2.49.
mantras.lit: (With lances, javelins, spears and clubs,) with swords, with axes and paṭṭiśas they fought with the Devī in the battle. And some hurled spears, some nooses; and likewise others —
mantras.tr: With lances and javelins, with spears and maces, with swords, axes and halberds, they fought the Goddess in that battle. Some hurled spears, others nooses; and still others —
mantras.tr_note: The opening phrase is carried over from 2.47b. ‘Halberds’ renders पट्टिश loosely. The verse ends on अपरे, whose action follows in 2.49.

comm.t: The asura host, mustered in 2.40–47, attacks all at once. The verse names a whole armoury — swords, axes, paṭṭiśas, spears, nooses — to show the full weight of the assault the Devī is about to cut down.
The weapons the asuras use are largely those the gods have just given the Devī (2.20–31: spear, noose, axe, sword). The battle is fought weapon against weapon, and the text will show hers prevailing.

flags.uncertain: अपरे can also be read within this verse as an elliptical third member (‘and others likewise [hurled other weapons]’). Here it is taken with 2.49, on the pattern of तथापरे in 2.57–58, where the clause clearly runs on.

sandhi.note: Visarga before t becomes s. So too ततः तानि → ततस्तानि.
Final i before a dissimilar vowel becomes y: -णि अ- → -ण्य-.
Final m before a consonant is written as anusvāra; likewise तां हन्तुं प्रचक्रमुः.

samasa.alt: Also a tṛtīyā tatpuruṣa, खड्गेन प्रहाराः ‘blows (dealt) with the sword’; the sense is the same.

morph.note: Perfect of प्र + √क्रम् (reduplication च-क्रम्, क → च). With an infinitive it means ‘set about (doing)’. Classical grammar puts प्र + √क्रम् ‘to begin’ in the ātmanepada (प्रचक्रमिरे); the parasmaipada is the common epic usage.
Infinitive in -तुम् (tumun) of √हन्, expressing purpose with a verb of beginning: ‘began to kill’.
चण्डी ‘the fierce (woman)’ with the suffix -क: Caṇḍikā, the name by which the Devī is most often called in the middle and last caritas.

mantras.anvaya: (अपरे) ते तु खड्गप्रहारैः तां देवीं हन्तुं प्रचक्रमुः। ततः सा देवी चण्डिका अपि तानि शस्त्राणि अस्त्राणि (च) —
mantras.anvaya_en: Two sentences. The first ends the asuras’ assault. The second has its subject (सा देवी चण्डिका) and objects (तानि शस्त्राणि अस्त्राणि) here and its verb (प्रचिच्छेद) in 2.50.
mantras.lit: And they set about to kill her, the Devī, with sword-strokes. She too, the Devī Caṇḍikā, then — those weapons and missiles —
mantras.tr: set out to cut the Goddess down with blows of the sword. Then the Goddess Caṇḍikā, in her turn, took those weapons and missiles —
mantras.tr_note: The second line has no verb of its own; ‘took’ in the readable version only bridges to ‘cut to pieces’ in 2.50, where the verb stands.

comm.t: The attack reaches its height: the asuras close in with swords to kill her. The second line turns at once to the Devī’s answer, which 2.50 completes: she cuts every weapon down.
The pair शस्त्र and अस्त्र is the standard division of weapons: śastra is held and wielded, astra is released — thrown, shot or discharged. Naming both says that no kind of weapon reached her.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) also names her Caṇḍikā (name 755, चण्डिका). In the Devī Māhātmya the name belongs above all to the warrior Goddess of these battle chapters.

sandhi.type: consonant sandhi inside the word (tuk before ch)
sandhi.note: After the short i of the reduplicated syllable, ch is doubled as cch (चि + छेद → चिच्छेद).
a + ā → ā. The same rule joins शस्त्र + अस्त्र in निजशस्त्रास्त्रवर्षिणी.

samasa.vigraha: निजानि शस्त्राणि अस्त्राणि च वर्षति इति (तच्छीला)
samasa.type: upapada tatpuruṣa (the second member a kṛt form in -इन्, णिनि, ‘habitually doing’); its first member: शस्त्रास्त्र, itaretara dvandva (शस्त्राणि च अस्त्राणि च), qualified by निज (karmadhāraya)
samasa.literal: she who rains her own weapons and missiles
samasa.sense: pouring out her own arms against theirs as she cuts theirs down

samasa.type: bahuvrīhi (its first member अनायस्त is a nañ tatpuruṣa: न आयस्तम्)
samasa.literal: she whose face is not strained

samasa.sense: the gods who hailed her (2.34) and the sages who praised her (2.35)
samasa.alt: Also read as a karmadhāraya, सुराः च ते ऋषयः च ‘divine seers’ (like देवर्षि). The dvandva fits 2.34–35, where gods and sages praise her separately.

morph.note: Perfect of √छिद्: the reduplicated syllable छि becomes चि (an aspirate is reduplicated unaspirated), and the root vowel takes guṇa (छेद) in the singular.
Passive present stem स्तूय- (√स्तु + yak, with the root vowel lengthened before -य-) and the participle ending -मान: ‘being praised’, with the praisers in the instrumental.
The agent suffix -इन् (णिनि) on √वृष् ‘to rain’ (guṇa वर्ष-) gives वर्षिन् ‘raining (by habit)’; the feminine adds -ई: वर्षिणी (n → ṇ after r).

mantras.anvaya: (सा देवी चण्डिका तानि शस्त्राणि अस्त्राणि) निजशस्त्रास्त्रवर्षिणी लीलया एव प्रचिच्छेद। अनायस्तानना सुरर्षिभिः स्तूयमाना देवी —
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line completes the sentence of 2.49b with its verb प्रचिच्छेद. The second line opens a new sentence whose verb, मुमोच, stands in 2.51.
mantras.lit: Raining her own weapons and missiles, she cut (them) to pieces merely in play. The Devī, her face unwearied, being praised by the gods and seers —
mantras.tr: and, raining down her own weapons and missiles, cut them to pieces as if in play. Unwearied of face, praised by gods and seers, the Goddess —
mantras.tr_note: The verse divides between two sentences; the dash marks the subject of 2.51.

comm.t: The point is effortlessness: लीलया एव ‘merely in play’ and अनायस्तानना ‘her face unstrained’. The whole armoury of 2.48 is undone without the Devī showing effort, while gods and seers look on and praise her.

The same phrase returns in the third carita: Caṇḍikā cuts Śumbha’s weapons चिच्छेद लीलया (8.31). The tradition hears in लीला the Devī’s freedom: what she does in the world is play, not labour or need.

Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has a close image in its own battle with Bhaṇḍa: name 79, भण्डासुरेन्द्रनिर्मुक्तशस्त्रप्रत्यस्त्रवर्षिणी, ‘she who rains counter-missiles against the weapons released by Bhaṇḍāsura’. Both texts use the same agent noun -वर्षिणी for the warrior Goddess; the battles themselves are different stories.

sandhi.note: Before a vowel सः is treated like any -aḥ: before a it becomes so, and the a of अपि is elided (avagraha).
-aḥ before a voiced consonant becomes -o (twice). -āḥ before the voiced v loses its visarga (देव्याः → देव्या), which is why the genitive looks like the instrumental.

samasa.literal: on the bodies of the asuras
samasa.sense: her weapons now strike the enemy themselves, not only their weapons

samasa.type: bahuvrīhi (the feminine सटा ‘mane’ is shortened to -सट as the last member of a bahuvrīhi qualifying a masculine)

samasa.sense: the lion given by Himavat as her vehicle (2.29)

morph.note: Perfect of √मुच्: reduplication मु-, guṇa of the root vowel in the singular (मोच). Its ātmanepada counterpart मुमुचे follows in 2.52.
Genitive singular of देवी. The verse prints देव्या because -āḥ drops its visarga before a voiced sound; the sense (‘the Devī’s mount’) shows it is the genitive, not the instrumental देव्या.
kta of √क्रुध्: dh + t → ddh (क्रुध् + त → क्रुद्ध). Intransitive, so active in sense: ‘angered’.

mantras.anvaya: (अनायस्तानना सुरर्षिभिः स्तूयमाना देवी) ईश्वरी असुरदेहेषु शस्त्राणि अस्त्राणि च मुमोच। देव्याः वाहनकेसरी सः अपि क्रुद्धः धुतसटः —
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line completes the sentence opened in 2.50b. The second begins a new one: subject (सः … वाहनकेसरी) with two qualifiers; its verb, चचार, is in 2.52.
mantras.lit: the Sovereign released weapons and missiles on the bodies of the asuras. He too, enraged, his mane shaken, the lion that was the Devī’s mount —
mantras.tr: loosed her weapons and missiles upon the asuras’ bodies, sovereign that she is. And her lion too, the Goddess’s own mount, raging and tossing his mane —

comm.t: Defence turns to attack: having destroyed the asuras’ weapons, the Devī now looses her own on their bodies. The lion given her by Himavat (2.29) enters the fight in his own right.
ईश्वरी, ‘sovereign’, is chosen at the moment she goes on the offensive: the battle is the exercise of her lordship, not a contest between equals.

samasa.alt: Also analysed as a ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa with अशन as an agent noun, हुतस्य अशनः ‘the eater of the oblation’; both analyses give the same name for fire.

morph.note: The ātmanepada perfect of √मुच्, beside the parasmaipada मुमोच of 2.51: √मुच् is ubhayapadin. The ātmanepada suits an action whose fruit stays with the agent — here, her own breath.
Present middle participle of √युध्: the divādi stem युध्य- + -मान (śānac). It is not passive; √युध् is itself ātmanepadin.

mantras.anvaya: (सः) वनेषु हुताशनः इव असुरसैन्येषु चचार। रणे युध्यमाना अम्बिका यान् च निःश्वासान् मुमुचे —
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line completes the lion’s sentence from 2.51b, with a simile. The second line is a relative clause (यान् … मुमुचे) whose main clause (ते एव … गणाः) is in 2.53.
mantras.lit: ranged among the asura armies like fire in forests. And the breaths which Ambikā, fighting in battle, released —
mantras.tr: raged through the asura ranks like a fire through the forests. And every breath that Ambikā breathed out as she fought —

comm.t: Two images of the Devī’s power multiplying. The lion goes through the army like a forest fire; and the Devī’s very breathing becomes a weapon, as the next verse shows.

The contrast with Mahiṣa is drawn by the text itself: in the next chapter Mahiṣāsura fells the Devī’s troops with the wind of his breath (निःश्वासपवनेन, 3.23). Her breath brings forth an army; his only destroys.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) also names her Ambikā (name 295, अम्बिका), ‘the Mother’ — the name the Devī Māhātmya uses most often in its battle scenes.
